report:
Based on the evidence gathered, here is my assessment.

**Conclusion: The claim is well supported and true, not false.** Multiple large observational studies and randomized/quasi-experimental designs consistently show that bystander hands-only (compression-only) CPR increases survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) compared with no bystander CPR at all.

**Key evidence:**
- A 2010 JAMA study of over 4,000 patients found survival to hospital discharge was 5.2% with no bystander CPR versus 7.8% for conventional CPR and 13.3% for compression-only CPR — a large, statistically significant benefit for hands-only CPR over doing nothing (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/186668).
- A PMC review similarly concluded that bystander-initiated compression-only CPR is better than no CPR, reinforcing this direction across studies (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3484593/).
- A systematic review notes bystander CPR (of any type) is associated with roughly 2.4-fold higher odds of survival to discharge compared to no CPR, and even in older adults the association remained positive (~24% higher survival) (https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacadv.2023.100607).
- Registry data (CARES, 194,807 witnessed OHCAs) show earlier bystander CPR of any kind is associated with improved survival compared with no bystander CPR at each time interval studied (https://www.resuscitationjournal.com/article/S0300-9572(25)00078-4/fulltext).

**Nuance — the real debate:** The controversy in recent literature is not "CPR vs. no CPR" but "compression-only vs. conventional (with breaths) CPR." Some newer meta-analyses find these two approaches roughly equivalent, and one recent analysis even favored standard CPR slightly (OR 1.22) over compression-only in longer-term outcomes. This debate does not undermine the original claim, which compares hands-only CPR to *no* CPR — a comparison for which evidence is strong and consistent.

**Bottom line:** The claim that hands-only CPR beats no bystander CPR is robustly supported by observational and registry evidence; it should not be considered false. The genuine scientific uncertainty lies elsewhere (compression-only vs. conventional CPR), not in this specific comparison.
